production.titleCard: Four principles, before we plan anything
production.note: The four principles and their "what it means in practice" lines are slide 12 and its notes, word for word. The opening and closing lines are Noy's wording. Stop 1 sits before "Start measuring badly..." (the first plan had it after the whole segment), so the film answers the question after the learner does.

segments.narration: You have a goal: fifteen percent more orders by March, at the same cost per order. A good goal. But how will you know you bought it?
Four principles, before we plan anything.
onScreen: Four principles, before we plan anything

segments.narration: Principle one: measure whether the goals were met, do not only act. Activity is not evidence. If you cannot name the number that proves a goal happened, it was an aspiration.

Principle two: measurement starts tactical and intuitive, then matures into precise insight. Nobody's first dashboard is right. Start measuring badly rather than not at all, and sharpen it every month.
segments.stopInside: stop1, after "Nobody's first dashboard is right."

segments.narration: Principle three: understand what works, what does not, which campaign failed, and which investment was profitable. All four, not just the first. A plan that only reports successes cannot be optimised.
onScreen: All four, not just the first

segments.narration: Principle four: building the measurement infrastructure is a necessary step before any marketing activity begins. Set it up before the campaign. Nobody sets up tracking retroactively. Data you do not collect today cannot be analysed in the future.
So before you spend anything, the tracking goes in. Now open your workbook: write your goal, and how and from when you will measure it.

challenges.text: A thorough understanding of the market, including competitors, demand and our own status. It is a lot of work and it is where most plans are already weak.
Discrepancies between what different functions inside the organisation want.
Short sales cycles against long ones. A plan built for one fails on the other.
Disparities between the strategy and the ability to actually execute it.
Execution competence: the inability to adapt to a market that is changing quickly.
“Everything is urgent”: no prioritisation in the work plan.
Following the buzz and reacting to the hype.
Measuring and monitoring capabilities, or the absence of them.

script.text: A few broad observations, and things worth arguing about.
Market education is an expensive strategy. Where demand exists, concentrate on it and find a focused way to meet it.
Long-tail organic traffic takes a lot of time and a lot of newly created content. It is not a shortcut.
Competing against major players, monopolies or dominant players is hard. Think partnerships, a different business model, or a large budget.
Viral marketing and social networks are not stable or predictable business models.
Is virality really not a business model?
Spread the investment across several marketing channels.
Build continuing synergy between the channels: social sharing helps SEO, organic optimisation helps paid keyword conversion, and so on.
It is difficult to get results if the website or the online activity does not have a clear purpose.
Next module you build that website.

screens.instruction: Four sentences that carry the whole lecture
stages: Before any other online marketing activity, the first step is market research, to understand the nature of the market, the customers and the competitors.
Gathering and analysing data is what forms the basis for genuinely understanding our market.
We can create a strategy and a work plan only after a market analysis that accounts for the competitors, the market's attributes, and the organisation's ability to respond.
We then formulate and manage a work plan that builds a marketing funnel with a range of powerful, quantifiable traffic sources.
